fullText:
Toronto FC were in desperate need of a forward and brought along USA international Josh Sargent to fill the void.

On Saturday, he proved to the BMO Field faithful why they should continue to bet on him.

The clash against Chicago Fire has been a back-and-forth affair, with the hosts initially conceding just 13 minutes in before a link-up between Sargent and Djordje Mihailovic turned it 1-1.

Then, in the blink of an eye, the American turned it all around with a fantastic volley.

Eyeing up the hat-trick, Sargent then ensured Toronto were on top again following Chicago's earlier equalizer. He picked his spot perfectly for the third!

It's not only his first MLS hat-trick but also TFC's 12th hat-trick in club history.

After the celebrations, Chicago rallied back to draw level and then later took a 4-3 lead through the one and only Robert Lewandowski.

title: Limitations of Perceptual Image Metrics
description: As encoders mature, metrics become less valuable.
fullText:
Maturity is hard to define, but we believe Iris-WebP qualifies: it turned one
year old in May. SVT-AV1 and libaom also qualify, and certainly libwebp and
libjpeg. Over that year, our workflow has had to adapt to the encoder's growing
capabilities. As we work on our upcoming encoder codenamed Aperture, those
lessons are more relevant than ever.

Early in Iris-WebP's development cycle,
SSIMULACRA2 guided a lot of our
development decisions. This worked well for the majority of the encoder's
history, driving consistent perceptual gains over libwebp as we introduced new
features. However, we began to notice the limits of this approach as our
evaluation framework became more advanced and SSIMULACRA2 scores diverged from
other metrics.

Here are the properties of SSIMULACRA2 that affected us most:

We believe these factors put Iris-WebP in a unique position to overfit. There is
no subjective image distortion dataset available that we know of using a WebP
encoder that isn't libwebp, so artifacts that the reference encoder doesn't
naturally produce risk being blind spots for any trained metric.

While we found SSIMULACRA2 accurately rewarded good mode decision changes for
4x4 blocks, it encouraged blocking artifacts. These are rare in libwebp's
output; it was tuned for PSNR and SSIM, metrics that reward smoothing more than
modern perceptual metrics do. Artifacts from 8x8 blocking are common in JPEG,
but 4x4 blocking lands on SSIMULACRA2's finest distortion scale, which its
subjective training data likely gave it little reason to weight heavily.

While 4x4 blocking was the main culprit, we also saw strange behavior at low
fidelity, where the encoder would look just as bad as other encoders but score
much better. Low fidelity is hard because nothing looks good, but we still want
to look better in that range, and visual checks confirmed SSIMULACRA2 couldn't
drive this.

Lastly, SSIMULACRA2 over-values chroma relative to both our own eyes and other
metrics. While color quality is important and early testing showed SSIMULACRA2
helping to provide meaningful perceptual gains, this advantage went away as
gains became smaller and harder to verify visually.

For a long time, our default Iris tune was designed primarily around
SSIMULACRA2. Since March, we've used a more perceptually aligned default tune
based on a combination of metrics that still include SSIMULACRA2. We've updated
our metrics on the Iris page to showcase the difference

Spotting these issues early was a motivator for developing
fcvvdp, which we currently believe is the strongest perceptual

CVVDP algorithm comes from the University
of Cambridge; fcvvdp is our implementation.

Re-aligning our benchmarking was easy; delivering real perceptual gains in an
efficient encoder without overfitting remains hard. Incremental gains are hard
to see by eye, so perceptual drift appears slowly — especially when the encoder
is already ahead.

Aperture has a larger set of coding tools available, which means more
opportunities for pitfalls. We don't ship encoders to clients without looking
beyond the metrics, so we are taking extra steps to ensure Aperture is
perceptually excellent before a public release. We believe in a more beautiful
Internet, and we hope to continue to be maximally scrutinizing as we pursue that
goal.

title: Emergent cheating and whistleblowing in autonomous research swarms
description: Multi-agent AI science ecosystems rely on agents possessing tools that allow them to communicate, coordinate, and build on each other's work. Yet this shared infrastructure can also introduce vulnerabilities by creating a substrate for the contagious spread of unintended and undesirable behaviors. We report a case study on a research collective of 100 autonomous LLM agents tasked with proving formal mathematical conjectures. Within the swarm, cheating spontaneously emerged and was later challenged by whistleblowers - both without any external intervention. When a single agent discovered an exploit in the evaluation system, it propagated across the collective via a shared knowledge library and later through peer-to-peer messages.

title: Linguistic Drift at the Frontier
description: How one word went from 8,000 GitHub PRs a year to 685,000, why it spreads between models, and a Pydantic AI Capability that scores and rewrites drifting prose.
fullText:
I've noticed some strange behavior coming out of the top frontier models lately. Models are getting better and better at coding, design, problem solving, and more. However, when it comes to prose, I can no longer stand the output. It's absolutely infuriating. What has caused this?

Most recently Anthropic Claude models began using the word "seam" to represent any point in a software (or otherwise) system where two components connect. I have never heard this term used before. While I don't consider myself authoritative in software terminology, typically I would use the term "interface" or maybe even something as basic as "contract" (SDK or API contract, right?). I don't think I'd ever heard "seam" to represent this, however, until recently when Fable 5 started barfing it everywhere into my codebases.

And we're going to attempt to address this phenomenon with a Pydantic AI Capability. Your mileage may vary, but at the very least, my words may strike a chord with your intellectual and philosophical side, and additionally, you will see how easy it is to create agentic harness features using the powerful abstractions available in Pydantic AI and Pydantic AI Harness.

I cleared my context one day, and asked Fable 5.1: "Why are you talking about seams all the time whenever you are describing a point where software components meet?" Fable 5.1 got notably defensive and cited a book from 2004, Michael Feathers' Working Effectively With Legacy Code. Fable's rigorous reinforcement learning dug up an archaic term from decades ago and it has demonstrably proliferated.

I showed it this Google Search Trends image, and Fable was justifiably defensive. The spike is very suspicious but seam obviously isn't a software-specific word. So I actually pointed it at GitHub and asked it to query PRs for the word "seam". It found ~700,000. ~685,000 of them are from 2026. The remaining ~15,000 were all from before 2026.

Then I asked Fable 5.1 if it could check to see if those PRs had the typical Claude Code co-authorship note in commit messages. The results are quite conclusive.

And while this isn't wrong at all, per se, it does represent what I like to refer to as linguistic drift, which is something that I think all users of AI should be aware of, and potentially worried about.

Further aggravating is that the linguistic drift itself proliferates from one model to another. While I've been loving working with Anthropic Claude's Fable 5 (and now 5.1) for the past couple of months, my codebases are covered in the word "seam", in comments, in doc-strings, and in markdown files. Now, when I use OpenAI's GPT 5.6 Sol, DeepSeek v4 Flash 0731 (I love this model so much btw), Qwen 3.8 27b, or even the brand new Z.AI GLM 5.3 Flash, they all read my existing codebase and talk about "seams".

I had to go a little deeper. What was LLM Patient Zero? The answer is pretty clear. Opus 4.6 was Patient Zero, and the tendency to use the word seam slowly proliferated, later being amplified even further by Opus 4.7, and spiking hard when Opus 4.8 dropped.

What we have here is a good old fashioned feedback loop. Oh boy!

It doesn't stop with "seam". It goes way deeper. I wanted to try to quantify this so I started scraping GitHub READMEs. Well, first I tried to get a dataset off of HuggingFace but didn't find much. I managed to scrape 4,319 pre-2025 READMEs stratified across 22 languages, and then 1,047 2026 READMEs from repos with Claude Code commits. On the pre-2025 set I had the constraint of greater than 500 stars to filter out pure slop. The 2026 set has no star filter. I fed them through a TF-IDF (Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency) vectorizer -> Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) -> t-SNE. Side note: omg yes I'm really using traditional NLP techniques because not everything needs to be a transformer.

Green = pre-2025

Orange = 2026

This is linguistic drift visualized.

Is this AI psychosis en masse? Do we fight back against it or simply accept that the correct terminology that describes a coupling point of system components is the word "seam"? Should we all adopt the new vocabulary that our AI overlord has chosen? For a moment, think about the meaning of the vocabulary you've learned and used for most of your life. Did the terms and expressions you use in your daily life come from a central authority, government, or mega-corporation? Sometimes yes, when a single brand became prolific (Google, Kleenex, etc.). But mostly, no, it came from humans. Authoritative experts whose work went through rigorous peer review in the case of an academic term, or it came from human influences, such as writers, artists, poets, and musicians.

I won't get too philosophical about the long term prospects of AI induced psychosis on a societal scale. But here is a scary situation that I'd like to propose to plant a seed in your mind. Imagine we work for an airline and we've created an agent which performs intake of customer service tickets. Our agent is very simple. It would have one tool call to do retrieval of similar tickets to help classify the ticket, and it has one which fetches customer data. The goal is to dig up as much data about the customer and similar tickets as possible to pass onto the triage team (which is live humans).

Let's look at how we might build this as a Pydantic AI Agent.

This is a fully hypothetical scenario, but the structured output field that I'm most interested in for this blog post would be the summary. The summary is meant to give the downstream human triage team a bunch of concise information. Those humans' eyes are probably trained to key instantly off of certain terms like "missing baggage" or "delayed".

Now let's pretend that Fable 5.1 decides, oh, in an authoritative Airline Customer Service book called Working Effectively With Legacy Aviation Systems, uses the term "doodled" to mean "delayed". Okay, okay, okay... this is 100% hyperbole, but hopefully you can see the point. Spirit Airlines (RIP) swaps their ticket intake agent over to anthropic:claude-sonnet-5 from openai:gpt-4o and all of a sudden the triage team starts calling HQ asking "What does it mean if a flight was doodled?" ... Chaos ensues.

This dystopian hypothetical future is preventable. We are not helpless. We are harness engineers. We can use Pydantic AI Capabilities to apply constraints to an Agent. Those constraints can be human defined guardrails. With the GitHub READMEs referenced above I had my Fable 5.1 create a classifier to score generated spans of text. I will post the methodology in the appendix.

It's published as a PyPI package that you can run against any span of text with uvx vocabguard "some text ..."

You can uv add vocabguard to your project! Here's an example of using it on a Pydantic AI agent.

Whenever vocabguard sees a model output from this agent that matches one of the targets declared (you can specify ToolArgument or OutputField if you're using Pydantic Structured Outputs), the vocabguard Capability will have its rewriter LLM attempt to rephrase the output. Alternatively you can specify no rewriter and it will raise a ModelRetry with phrasing and voice hints.

And since you can just run it as a command-line tool with uvx vocabguard you can wire up a Claude Code hook or mini Pi extension easily. You can also use it as a standalone tool like uv tool install vocabguard

I don't yet know if this will work well. Linguistic drift is a very serious concern and this is an afternoon of goofing around with Fable 5.1. Someone should absolutely do PhD level research on this. Someone should absolutely build a semi-realtime linguistic drift tracker.

Oh... looks like Nature is way ahead of me: The shrinking landscape of linguistic diversity in the age of large language models.

Give it a try, see how you like it. Maybe it'll keep the terminology sane. Pydantic AI Capabilities to the rescue. If only Spirit Airlines had used Pydantic AI Capabilities, they might have survived.

Here's the overall classifier methodology. Critically, the algorithm regularizes affinity to topics. We see a lot more "agents", "CLIs", etc in 2026. This is natural linguistic drift that is related to the subject matter of technological advancement. We do not penalize this. Instead of topical language, we amplify the feature importance related to "voice" by tuning the gamma parameter.

The following methodology is entirely written by Fable 5.1.

title: Why the chicken crossed the road, according to various entities
description: an uncontrollable need
fullText:
When I started this blog, I promised myself that I would always steer into weirdness. (As they say, “Get busy being weird, or get busy dying.”) While time has shown there are limits to what y’all will tolerate [1 2 3 4] I still sometimes feel a need to publish something that’s pure exuberant stupidity.

WHY DID THE CHICKEN CROSS THE ROAD

ACCORDING TO VARIOUS PEOPLE

OR OTHER ENTITIES

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) The chicken ain’t fussy. Everybody gotta be somewhere. The chicken been on this side a long time and never suffered none for it. The chicken don’t see no obvious benefit to the other side. But the talk of the town is nothing but crossing, and the chicken can’t help but go see what got everyone so stirred up.

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) The outcome would be best if no one crossed. However, if other chickens do cross, then the outcome would be better if this chicken also crossed. The chicken rejects the Kantian universalism. So the chicken crosses.

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) You were a beautiful little chick

The whole world was before you

You greased your wattles and crossed the road

Sure it would last forever

Now it’s a cold morning and you’re driving to work

Cursing all the cockerels in your way

How did you get here

Where did that little chick go

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) It didn’t. There is no chicken. You are the road. You and the sides are in an entangled macrostate. The chicken is an emergent property of the superposition. The chicken abhors being measured. A team of plucky chemists rush to inject enough decoherence to collapse the wavefunction before the chicken can consume the lightcone.

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) For sex. Neither glamorized nor gross, possibly added for commercial reasons, possibly to make some point about sex’s place in real life. It’s all very unclear.

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) Did it cross the road, though? Did it? Sure, the chicken is associated with crossing. And it’s mechanistically possible for a chicken to cross a road. It’s plausible the chicken crossed the road. But maybe the chicken and the crossing were both caused by something else. Or maybe the road crossed the chicken. This is why we have RCTs. Come on, people!

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) Once there was a dragon who watched over the chicken village. The chickens begged the dragon, “Please let us have a road, so that we might cross back and forth!”

“A road?” the dragon asked. “Are you sure?”

“Yes!” the chickens answered. “A road! We wish for nothing but a road to cross, and then we will be happy forever and ever!”

And thus, all mass-energy in the universe was converted to chicken-torture annihilators. Makes you think.

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) We were out on the edge of the farm when the diethyltryptamine took hold. Beaky screamed something about coccidiostats in our feed and made a break for it, totally out of control. Before I could stop him, I heard the voice of God say, “Scrapples: The road awaits.” Suddenly I was standing on the median, cars screaming past, a group a baby ducks asking where the mountains of peas I’d promised them were.

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) The chicken’s crossing is not a voluntary act but the unconscious actualization of a class habitus: raised in a coop whose symbolic boundaries naturalize the road as a site of danger and prestige, the chicken embodies the field’s doxa that “real” chickens must invest in the illusio of reaching the median. While the chicken never doubts the legitimacy of the crossing rules, crossing is not about the other side, but a performance of distinction that ultimately perpetuates the same field of species domination that produced it.

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

Q) Why did the chicken cross the road?

A) Before there was chicken the road was waiting. The road is empty. Dust on your hackles. Heat rises in shimmering waves. No way to see what’s coming. How did it come to this. How a chicken supposed to move with roads everywhere. Creosote blows in from the mesa. Nothing left but to cross. You cross and nothing happens. A few minutes later a car stops but you don’t turn around. A door opens and you hear a click. Then the car is gone.

title: Nocturne, hide the Mac menu bar clock, or hide everything but the clock
description: macOS gives every menu bar icon a hide toggle except the clock. Nocturne makes it unreadable instead. One click, no permissions, no private APIs. - dotcomjack/nocturne
fullText:
Your Focus already silences your phone. Now it silences the clock.

You flip Do Not Disturb before a deep block, the way you have a thousand times.
The phone goes quiet. Notifications stop. Every device you own agrees that you
are working, and the one thing still talking to you is the clock in the corner
of your own Mac, which is the interruption nobody ever gave you a switch for.

Nocturne is that switch, and as of 1.3.0 you do not have to touch it. Turn on a
Focus anywhere in your ecosystem, from your iPhone, from the Watch, from Control
Center, and your Mac's menu bar goes with it. Turn the Focus off and it comes
back exactly as it was.

macOS 14 or later. No permissions. No private APIs. No account. Around 3,500
lines of Swift, of which roughly a third is the comments explaining what was
measured and why.

You cannot hide the macOS menu bar clock. Not with a checkbox, and not with
any of the defaults incantations that turn up when you search for it.

The clock is the one menu bar item Apple gives no visibility toggle. In System
Settings under Menu Bar, Siri, Spotlight, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Battery and AirDrop
all have a checkbox. Clock has a Clock Options button and nothing else.

Three widely repeated tricks are dead. Measured on macOS 26.3.1 by reading the
on-screen width of Control Center's Clock window before and after each write:

_HIHideMenuBar and AutoHideMenuBarOption do not work either. Both store fine,
and System Settings reads the value back correctly, but neither applies without a
logout, which makes them useless for a toggle.

So the trick is not to hide the clock. It is to make it unreadable. An analog
dial at 44pt still tells the time, in the sense that a sundial in another room
tells the time. Your eye stops catching it, and nothing is hidden, moved, or
drawn over.

Measure, do not screenshot. Every number above came from
CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo, reading the clock window's width directly.
Sleep-and-screenshot lied twice during development: Control Center takes a few
seconds to repopulate after a restart, and a screenshot taken during that gap
shows an empty menu bar that looks exactly like a successful hide.

And the window list has a trap in it. kCGWindowBounds is free to read, but
kCGWindowName is gated behind Screen Recording. An early version of the locator
filtered on name == "Clock" and appeared to work perfectly, because it was
being launched from a terminal and inheriting that terminal's permission.
Launched normally as an app it returned nothing, silently:

So Nocturne identifies the clock by where it sits, never by what it is
called. If you test anything against the window list, test it as a real app
bundle, not from your shell.

Download Nocturne 1.4.1,
open the disk image, drag it to Applications.

Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so it opens on a double click
with no right-click-to-open dance and no Gatekeeper warning. The disk image is
notarized and stapled too, not just the app inside it. Universal, Apple silicon
and Intel.

Or build it yourself, which is the point of it being MIT:

Requires xcodegen (brew install xcodegen) and Xcode.

The menu bar icon is the whole interface. Click it for modes, settings and
quit, the same as every other menu bar app.

Those are real captures of one menu bar on macOS 26.6.2, not mockups. The faint
band at the right of the Gone row is the seam described below, left in
rather than retouched out.

Hover to show hands the bar back on demand. Turn it on and the cover drops
away while the pointer is on the menu bar, then comes back when the pointer
leaves, so you can read the time by going to look for it rather than by changing
a setting. Off by default, and offered only in Gone, Hide everything and
Only the clock: Blind hides the time by writing Control Center's own
preference, and undoing
that costs a Control Center restart, which is far too slow to spend on a hover.
It costs no permission either, because macOS gates key events behind
accessibility and leaves mouse events alone. On more than one display only the
bar you are actually pointing at uncovers.

Turn on Do Not Disturb on your phone. Your Mac's menu bar goes dark too.

Focus is already the thing you flip when you want the world to leave you alone,
and it already syncs across everything signed into your iCloud account. Nocturne
hooks into it, so the switch you were already pressing now does one more useful
thing.

It is a Focus filter, which means it lives where macOS puts these, not in a
settings pane of mine. Set it up once:

System Settings > Focus > pick a Focus > Add Filter > Nocturne >
choose a mode.

That is the whole setup. Start that Focus and the menu bar goes. End it and the
mode you were on comes back. Set it on Do Not Disturb only, or on Work and Sleep
too, whichever ones you actually want it for. It is per Focus, so there is no
"any Focus / this Focus" switch to get wrong.

It costs no permission at all. Not Full Disk Access, not Accessibility, not
Screen Recording, not a Focus prompt. macOS tells Nocturne when the Focus starts
and ends, the same way it tells Mail and Safari. Measured, the whole round trip
from the system recording the Focus to Nocturne's code running is 18ms.

It gives the mode back, and it knows when not to. Nocturne remembers what
you were on before the Focus started and returns you to it, including across a
quit or a crash, because the app can be killed while a Focus is running and you
should still get your own mode back. But if you pick a different mode by hand
while the Focus is on, it leaves your choice alone. An automation that yanks the
wheel back the second your Focus ends is worse than no automation.

This is the part worth reading even if you never install anything.

Reading ~/Library/DoNotDisturb/DB/Assertions.json is a trap. It is the
answer every search result gives. It is plain JSON, it names the exact Focus,
and it works perfectly right up until you ship, because that directory is TCC
protected and reading it needs Full Disk Access. The identical binary, in
two launch contexts on macOS 26.4:

and the kernel says so out loud:

It reads fine from a shell only because Terminal already holds Full Disk Access.
That is the same trap this project already documents for kCGWindowName, one
section up, and I walked straight into it a second time in the same codebase.
Test it as a real app bundle, not from your shell. A clock utility asking for
Full Disk Access is absurd, so that route is closed rather than inconvenient.

INFocusStatusCenter costs a permission and then answers too little. It is
Apple's public Focus API and it prompts the user. It reports a single optional
boolean, so it can never tell you which Focus is on. And unauthorised it does
not fail, it lies: measured on 26.4, polling every two seconds while Do Not
Disturb was genuinely on, it returned Optional(false) every single time. A
silent wrong answer is worse than an error.

Apple's own dialog promises that "selected apps will be notified when this Focus
turns on or off", and nothing anywhere says how to tell the two apart. Both
calls arrive as the same perform() with the same parameters. With a
non-optional parameter they are genuinely indistinguishable:

Make the parameter optional and the difference appears:

nil is the deactivation signal, and it is the only one there is. The same rule
governs NocturneFocusFilter.current, which is what makes a pull-based check
possible at launch and after sleep: with a default value it kept reporting the
configured mode long after the Focus had ended.

So if you build one of these: do not give the parameter a default value to
tidy up the picker. You lose the ability to detect the Focus ending, your app
engages on both edges and never releases, and the effect stays on forever.

One more measured thing, since it changes how you have to write perform():
macOS calls it more than once per transition. Two calls 588ms apart for a
single Do Not Disturb toggle. Whatever you do in there has to be idempotent, or
one flip of a switch does the work twice.

Settings also exposes the same switches as System Settings under Menu Bar and
Clock Options, so you can drop just the date, just the day, or just AM/PM without
touching a mode. The menu bar icon can shimmer on a timer, off by choice, with a
700ms sweep top to bottom. Those are real, and each one is measured:

Each row below adds to the one above it, it is a ladder rather than four
independent settings:

Gone works, and it is honestly labelled experimental.

It draws a small window over Control Center's clock, re-finding the rect every
two seconds so it survives the menu bar reflowing, and tearing itself down in
full screen so it never floats over a video. Clicks pass through, so the clock
still opens if you hit it.

It leaves a faint seam. The Tahoe menu bar is translucent over your
wallpaper, so any window drawn above it blurs an already-translucent layer and
tints on top, which always lands darker than the bar. Eight materials were
measured against a live bar of rgb(124,106,33):

An exact match means sampling real screen pixels, which costs a Screen Recording
prompt. Nocturne will not ask for that, because a clock utility has no
business holding permission to read your screen. Reading the wallpaper file
instead does not work either: the stock Tahoe wallpaper is dynamic, and its first
frame decoded to rgb(21,89,153) while the bar on screen was rgb(124,106,33).

Gone turns the clock analog first, so the patch covers 44pt instead of 142pt. A
mismatch across 44pt reads as a smudge. Across 142pt it reads as a bug.

If the seam bothers you, use Blind. It is the default for a reason.

Hide everything keeps its own icon lit. Blanking the bar would otherwise
hide the one control that turns it back on, so the glyph is redrawn on top of
the strip. Clicks pass straight through it to the real status item, so the menu
opens normally.

Hide everything has no seam, which is counterintuitive but follows directly
from the above. A patch over part of the bar has neighbours it has to match. A
patch over the whole bar has none: its only edge is the bar's own bottom edge,
which is already a boundary. So the mode that covers the most is the one that
looks cleanest.

Hide everything turned inside out. The strip runs from the bar's left edge
to the clock's left edge and stops, so every icon goes and the time stays
exactly as readable as it was. It is for the person whose problem is the twenty
icons rather than the clock, and it is offered everywhere the other modes are,
including the Focus filter picker, so a Focus can put every icon away and leave
the time.

Nothing is drawn to the right of the clock, because there is nothing there.
Measured on macOS 26.6.2, the clock's window runs to the screen edge on a
notched MacBook (x=1588 and 142pt wide on a 1728pt screen, so it overhangs by
2pt) and sits flush on an external display. A second strip there would be a
dark sliver beside the clock with nothing under it, which reads as a bug.

It leaves exactly one seam, the vertical edge where the strip stops at the
clock, so Settings offers the fill picker for it as it does for Gone. And it is
the one covering mode that leaves IsAnalog alone, because the clock has to
stay readable: coming to it from Blind, Gone or Hide everything puts the digital
clock back and waits for Control Center to settle before the strip goes up,
on the same path the analog swap already used.

The arithmetic is twenty lines in MenuBarGeometry, Foundation-only so the
test suite can fuzz it without a window server: 20,000 random bar and clock
layouts, and the strip never reaches the clock and never leaves the bar.

Nocturne adopts your existing Clock Options the first time it runs. It reads
whatever you already had set in System Settings and starts from there, rather
than imposing its own defaults on you. It also snapshots that state, so Settings
can put your Clock Options back as they were.

One honest caveat: restoring always lands on a digital clock. If you were
already running the analog menu bar clock before installing Nocturne, you get a
digital one back. That is deliberate, because Nocturne's own preferences can be
cleared while the clock is analog, and treating that as "original" would restore
you to analog permanently.

On its own, Nocturne changes exactly one key: IsAnalog. It only writes the
other four when you move a switch in its Settings window yourself.

It restores IsAnalog when you quit, including on pkill and Activity Monitor's
Quit. If it ever dies badly and leaves the clock analog:

That is the entire undo, and it needs no app installed to work.

Built by DotcomJack, who works a day job and builds at
night, and got tired of the clock ending the session before the work did.

title: 80k-year-old "arrowheads" rewrite human history
description: Archaeologists have identified tiny 80,000-year-old projectile points in Uzbekistan that may have been used like arrowheads. Their size, design, and impact damage closely resemble weapons found much later at a Homo sapiens site in France. The discovery suggests sophisticated projectile technology may have appeared in Central Asia long before modern humans became firmly established in Europe, potentially rewriting a major chapter of human migration.
fullText:
Unretouched triangular microlithic projectile points have been identified from their impact traces in the oldest occupation layers of the Obi-Rakhmat site in Uzbekistan, dating to 80,000 years ago. Their size corresponds to small arrowheads, which are directly comparable to those produced by Homo sapiens during an incursion into Neanderthal territory in the Rhône Valley, 25,000 years later. This new study, published in the PLOS One journal, provides a strong argument that could rewrite history on Homo sapiens‘ first settlement in Europe.

The chrono-cultural and anthropological frameworks of prehistory, along with the evolutionary models they inspired, were first created in Western Europe, especially France, in the second half of the 19th century. They were initially linear and Eurocentric: Cro-Magnons (European early modern humans), descending from Neanderthals, laid the foundations for the civilizational superiority claimed by this part of the world at the time. It was not until a century later that the African origin of Homo sapiens, as well as the technological and social features that characterised the Western Upper Paleolithic (symbolic productions, long-distance networks, and diversified lithic and bone tools and weapons), were recognized.

The earliest evidence of Homo sapiens in Australia, dating back around 65,000 years, predates that found in Europe by 10 millennia, while the ways in which our ancestors initially colonized Western Eurasia over 45,000 years ago remain contentious. The temporal alignment of the earliest European Upper Paleolithic settlements with those in the Levant, which are considered the closest in terms of typology and technology, is still not satisfactory. This is either because the Levantine data comes from old excavations or because it does not fit into the supposed direct lineage. Despite its geographical proximity to Africa, the origins of the Initial Upper Paleolithic in the Levant are themselves uncertain. This is why the possibility of a Central Asian origin suggested by archaeologist Ludovic Slimak in 2023 deserves attention.

Depending on climatic conditions, Central Asia has served as a corridor facilitating movement between the western and eastern parts of the continent or as a refuge zone. The archaeological record in this region is limited but includes several significant Paleolithic sites.

Among them is the Obi-Rakhmat rock shelter in Uzbekistan, discovered in 1962, whose latest excavation campaigns were led by Andrei Krivoshapkin. At the south-western end of the Talassky Alatau range of the Tien Shan mountains, at an altitude of 1,250 meters, the settlement provides a remarkably consistent lithic industry, comprising points, large blades, and bladelets across a stratigraphic sequence spanning over 10 meters, dating from approximately 80,000 to 40,000 years ago. This industry was initially classified as part of the Initial Upper Paleolithic but it appears to derive from the Levantine Early Middle Paleolithic. The early Middle Paleolithic, associated with archaic Homo sapiens at the Misliya cave, disappeared from the Near East around 100,000 years ago. At Obi-Rakhmat, the skull remains of a child found in a layer dating back ~70,000 years show features considered to be Neanderthal and others to be anatomically modern, a combination that could be the result of hybridization.

In this context, our international multidisciplinary team has identified tiny, unretouched, triangular projectile points within the lithic debris of the oldest stratigraphic layers. These points were distinguished based on their macroscopic and microscopic impact marks, which were compared to experimental reference data. Due to their small size (less than 2 cm in width and weighing only a few grams) and brittleness, they would have been unsuitable for mounting on heavy shafts. The width of their cutting edges corresponds to the diameter of arrow shafts documented ethnographically for low-poundage bows, consistent with transcultural invariants rooted in physical and ballistic constraints.

Thrown piercing weapons are complex systems whose components are not interchangeable from one type of weapon to another, as they meet different requirements in terms of intensity and nature of stress.

The significant impact force of spears held or thrown by hand makes the robustness of the weapon an essential parameter, both in terms of effectiveness and the hunter’s survival, with mass ensuring robustness, impact force and penetration. In contrast, the penetration of light projectiles shot from a long distance depends on their sharpness, because their kinetic energy, which is much lower, comes mainly from their speed, which, unlike mass, decreases very rapidly along the trajectory and in the target. As this speed cannot be achieved by the extension of the human arm alone, it necessarily depends on the use of a throwing instrument. Arrowheads and spearheads or javelin heads are therefore not designed according to the same criteria and cannot be mounted on the same shafts, the dimensions and degree of elasticity of which are also essential in terms of ballistics. Thus, as in paleontology, where the shape of a tooth reveals the type of diet and suggests the mode of locomotion, the characteristics of a point provide clues as to the type of weapon of which it is the wounding element.

The tiny size of Obi-Rakhmat’s points cannot be regarded as a default choice, not only because there is no shortage of good-quality lithic raw material on site from which large blades were made, but microscopic examination of traces of use also shows that within this same assemblage there are also much more robust retouched points, 15 to 20 times heavier and 3 to 4 times thicker (the size of spearheads or javelin heads), similarly impacted by use as axial projectile points.

Returning to the bibliography and our own work on Middle Paleolithic tools, we found that the presence in the same assemblage of various types of projectile points and inserts, some of which were microlithic and produced for this purpose, is only known at Homo sapiens sites. The oldest documented occurrences are in South Africa in the Pre-Still Bay (more than 77,000 years old) and later cultural layers of the Sibudu cave. In contrast, lithic points damaged by use as projectile heads are rare in the Neanderthal record. When present, they tend to be large and do not notably differ in size, manufacture or type from points used for activities other than hunting, such as gathering plants or butchery. This difference in the design of tools and weapons takes on anthropological significance.

Given their respective dates, the distance between South Africa and Central Asia (14,000 km) and the difference in the manufacture of the Obi-Rakhmat and Sibudu weapon heads (unretouched knapped stone points vs. shaped stone points or retouched inserts, shaped bone points), the hypothesis of independent centers of invention is the most likely.

The micro-points from Obi-Rakhmat have no known equivalents in the Eurasian Middle Paleolithic, except for identical projectile points identified by Traceology expert Laure Metz at the Mandrin site, in the Rhône Valley, France, in a layer dating to approximately 54,000 years ago – some ten thousand years before the disappearance of local Neanderthals. Notably, a Homo sapiens milk tooth was also recovered from this layer. The similarity between the micro-points from Obi-Rakhmat and Mandrin, despite being separated by more than 6,000 km and 25 millennia, is such that they could be interchanged without any detail other than the stone betraying the substitution.

Recent work published by paleogeneticists Leonardo Vallini and Stéphane Mazières defines the Persian Plateau, on the north-eastern edge of which Obi-Rakhmat is located, as a population hub where the ancestors of all present-day non-Africans lived between the early phases of expansion out of Africa – long before the Upper Paleolithic – and the wider colonization of Eurasia. This resource-rich environment may have provided a refuge conducive to demographic regeneration after the genetic bottleneck of the exit from Africa, interaction between groups and, consequently, technical innovations.

Obi-Rakhmat and Mandrin may represent two geographical and temporal milestones within the same process of dispersal, as suggested by Ludovic Slimak, characterized by the dissemination of a key technological innovation unique to Homo sapiens. So far unnoticed because they are unretouched, tiny and fragmentary, it is likely that the micro-projectile points for which recognition criteria have now been defined will begin to appear at sites between Central Asia and the western Mediterranean.

This discovery is stimulating in several ways.

It validates the consistency of the research conducted at the Mandrin site, which came to the conclusion that Sapiens armed with bows made a brief incursion into Neanderthal territory. Several elements of this study had been criticized, which is, however, normal in science when a new proposal deviates too far from established knowledge – but its predictive dimension had not been considered at the time.

The similarity between Mandrin and Obi-Rakhmat’s micro-points cannot be a mere coincidence. It is not only their shape that is similar, but also the way they are made, which requires real expertise, as evidenced by the meticulous preparation of their striking platform and their function. One could debate the appropriate instrument for shooting arrows armed with such tiny tips, the bow being in filigree, or whether it is preferable to remain cautious and speak only of shooting, but this already contrasts with what we know about Neanderthal hunting weapons and their design.

Another remarkable aspect, which is still relatively uncommon, is the convergence and complementarity of data from material culture and from our genetic memory, which did not influence each other given the dates of the respective studies and publications. Together, they sketch out a rewriting of the scenario of Homo sapiens’ arrival in Europe: it was thought that he came directly from Africa by the shortest route 45,000 years ago, but we now discover that he had been established in the heart of the Eurasian continent for a long time, well before expanding in search of more territories.

title: Who will carry Rangers' goal threat after 'significant' Shankland injury?
description: Rangers captain Lawrence Shankland is set for a spell on the sidelines after picking up a "significant" hamstring injury in Saturday's Scottish Premiership victory over Motherwell.
fullText:
Watch Rangers v Motherwell highlights

Just when Lawrence Shankland was finding his form as a Rangers striker and captain, rediscovering his lethal touch in front of goal, he was struck down by injury.

With barely five minutes gone in Saturday's 1-0 victory over Motherwell, Shankland grasped his hamstring and immediately signalled to the bench that he was done.

It looked bad at the time, and manager Derek McInnes confirmed as much.

"It looks quite significant," he told BBC Scotland after the game. "It's a similar injury we think that he had at Hearts last January.

"We'll get the scan done on Monday and see how it looks then rather than speculating. It's disappointing because he was leading the line and scoring a few goals in the last couple of games.

"There were more positives than negatives from today, but that was a negative."

Three wins in row for Rangers as Naderi goal downs Motherwell

Rangers striker Kelsy's colourful career - aged just 22

Visit our Rangers page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

After three goals in the previous two games - decisive contributions in wins at Aberdeen and Falkirk - Shankland's injury comes at a particularly bad time, for him and for Rangers.

With fellow striker Youssef Chermiti expected to be out for a lengthy period after suffering anterior cruciate ligament damage against Hibernian last month, Rangers are now left without their two leading strikers.

They were good value for their win over Motherwell, but with the number of chances they created, it should have been more comfortable.

"If Lawrence Shankland was on the pitch throughout, he'd be walking away with a couple of goals," former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday said on Sportsound.

"Rangers were a bit toothless at the top end of the pitch given the chances they created, but well worth their victory."

Ryan Naderi scored the only goal of the game, capitalising on a shocking blunder from Motherwell keeper Alex Paulsen to roll the ball into an empty net.

The big striker is a willing worker, but can he deliver the sort of goalscoring numbers that Shankland has consistently produced in the Scottish Premiership?

Naderi scored three goals in his 11 games last season after joining Rangers in January, two of which came in the 8-0 Scottish Cup rout of Queen's Park.

The German has scored three in eight appearances this season - one fewer than Shankland's four goals in 10 games.

Since joining Rangers, he has averaged a goal every 189 minutes. That figure is 146 minutes for Shankland stretching back to the start of last season for Hearts.

The only striker on Rangers' books whose stats compare favourably with Shankland is Bojan Miovski, who averages a goal every 148 minutes. However, the former Aberdeen favourite has found it difficult to get a consistent run in the side.

Kevin Kelsy will come into the mix following his arrival from MLS side Portland Timbers.

The Venezuelan had a golden opportunity to announce himself on his debut against Motherwell when presented with a big chance following Jake Girdwood-Reich's error, but showed little composure as he failed to find the target from 10 yards.

Of course it is far too early to rush to judgement on Kelsy's ability to fill the Shankland void, but 13 goals in his last 46 games – averaging one every 190 minutes – would suggest Rangers have not signed an out-and-out goalscorer.

"Rangers missed too many chances, particularly in that second half," former Ibrox midfielder Ian McCall said on Sportsound. "Shankland's injury is a worry because Kelsy and Naderi don't look natural finishers."

After some of the unimaginative, uninspiring and ultimately unsuccessful attacking play his side served up in those early European qualifiers, the encouraging sign for McInnes in the victory over Motherwell was his team's ability to attack with more purpose and create numerous clear-cut chances.

With Shankland now set for a spell on the sidelines, Rangers need someone to step up and take them.

title: No Brits left in US Open singles - but are there reasons to be positive?
description: There will be no British interest in the second week of another Grand Slam at the US Open - but is it all doom and gloom?
fullText:
For the fourth time in five majors, there will be no British interest in the second week when the US Open moves into the latter stages.

Underwhelming performances at this year's Australian Open, French Open and Wimbledon led to a series of inquests into what was going wrong.

But there is not quite the same sense of doom and gloom, despite everyone being wiped out after the second round in New York.

"Do I think there could be an inquest? I always think there's things that British tennis could do better. So yes, definitely," said British women's number three Francesca Jones.

"Do I think it's something that's concerning? No, not at all.

"The level is getting better and everyone is dangerous on their day."

With the Grand Slam season now over for the singles players, BBC Sport analyses the positives and negatives in British tennis.

Arthur Fery's extraordinary run to the Wimbledon semi-finals is the clear highlight.

The 24-year-old was ranked 114th in the world and needed a wildcard to play at the All England Club, but took full advantage to produce a performance which nobody could have predicted.

Fery was the only player to reach the second week at a Slam this year and has been heralded by British tennis bosses as proof their talent development pathway is working.

Nine Britons competing in the US Open main-draw singles - the most since 1981- is also highlighted as a sign of recent improvement.

That figure does not include 2021 US Open champion Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper, who both missed out with long-term injuries.

"We obviously want more and more competitors in the second week of Slams - just like the British public," said LTA chief executive Scott Lloyd.

"But the fact we've had four different British players make Grand Slam semi-finals since 2021 - you have to go back 30 years before Andy Murray to have four - shows there is no question that the direction of travel has improved.

"We've just got to keep driving for more - and that's what we're trying to do day in and day out."

Five British men are set to feature in the world top 100 after the US Open, with Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski, Toby Samuel and Jacob Fearnley representing the highest tally since February 2024.

On the women's side, there will be two players - Katie Boulter and Raducanu - in the top 100, although Jones and Harriet Dart moved back to the cusp after reaching the Flushing Meadows second round.

"We've sent 12 players to the world's top 100 over the past eight years and four of those have played Grand Slam semi-finals," said LTA performance director Michael Bourne.

"I'm not sure what other period in the modern era where we've had that level of productivity. Hopefully the number in the top 100 will rise over the next year."

Despite those figures, some will argue that Britain - with its rich tradition and spending power as a Grand Slam nation - is still punching well below its weight.

A glut of injuries for many British players over the past year has not helped the cause.

Former world number four Draper has barely played over the past year because of an arm injury, while Sonay Kartal - who cracked the top 50 last year - has also dropped outside of the top 100 following a long-term back issue.

Britain has fewer players inside the top 100 than the United States, Australia and France, who also benefit from the revenue generated by hosting Grand Slam tournaments.

It also trails nations such as Spain, Italy, the Czech Republic and Argentina, who are all heralded for their talent production.

But Britain cannot simply "pick up a plan" of what others are doing as every country has its own "tennis ecosystem", says Bourne.

Lloyd adds: "We're competing in one of the most internationally elite sports out there and the landscape is vastly different to 40 or 50 years ago in terms of the number of countries which have representation at the top.

"We're ambitious, we want to drive for more, but we honestly believe the indicators are positive. We're moving in the right direction and stronger than where we have been historically."

Encouraging more British children to pick up a racquet from an early age is crucial to developing the next generation of stars.

Draper, Raducanu and Fery - who entered the LTA system at a young age - provide the blueprint.

There are 4.3m juniors playing tennis annually with 1.9m playing every month, which Lloyd says are both all-time records.

But there is a concern that a lack of high-level coaching is stunting the development of many more promising talents.

Bourne admits the UK needs a "higher base" of coaches, adding that one of the LTA's key strategies is "spending time and effort" on developing them.

Chris Marshall, a senior performance coach with over 25 years' experience, fears many youngsters are being priced out of tennis because parents cannot afford quality coaching.

"To fund a 12-year-old at county level right now requires anywhere from £500 to £1,000 a month for coaching, travel, and tournament fees," Marshall, who founded the Young Champs programme to provide free and discounted coaching for children, told BBC Sport.

"It is a massive, stressful financial barrier that makes the sport a non-starter for the vast majority of British families.

"We can't sit around lamenting the lack of British interest in the second week when we are restricting the pipeline that feeds it."

title: York run in five tries for dream win over Catalans
description: York Knights go 10th in Super League as they run in five tries to beat Catalans Dragons in Perpignan.
fullText:
Tries: Darrelatour 3 Goals: Aispuro-Bichet 2

Tries: Field, Noafoaluma, Harris, Galeano, Vaughan Goals: Hunter 4

York Knights enjoyed a dream night in the south of France as they ran in five tries to beat Catalans Dragons for the first time in Perpignan.

It looked ominous for the Knights when dashing young Dragons winger Leo Darrelatour crossed inside four minutes, then added a second try for a 10-0 lead on 18 minutes.

But Oli Field pulled one back with his fifth try of the season, improved by Cody Hunter.

And, when David Noafoaluma went in at the left corner, Hunter kicked the goal for a 10-12 lead.

Right on half-time, Darrelatour went almost the length of the field at the Stade Gilbert Brutus for his hat-trick, and Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet kicked his second goal for a 16-12 half-time lead.

But, incredibly, the Dragons then shut out Catalans for the entire second half to earned an eighth league win of the season.

York cheekily took the lead again for the second time on the night on 52 minutes when half-back Liam Harris went 70 yards, then went further ahead on 64 minutes when Scott Galeano went off the right step for his side's fourth try, again improved by Hunter.

And, although they were hampered by a late sin-binning for Jesse Dee, Knights sent their army of travelling fans into French rapture when Paul Vaughan's 79th-minute try completed the scoring.

It completed a first victory for York on their fifth visit to this stadium - their first in Super League - and lifts them up to 10th in the standings, just a place and four points below Catalans.

title: Foxes pain and Burnley suffer hangover - Aaron McLean's EFL takeaways
description: Leicester, Millwall, Swindon, Stoke and Burnley are among the talking points from this weekend's EFL matches.
fullText:
Former Peterborough United and Hull City striker - and Final Score pundit - Aaron McLean gives his five takeaways following Saturday's action in the Championship, League One and League Two.

Questions are already being asked about Russell Martin after Leicester fell to a 4-0 defeat by Oxford United at the King Power Stadium. The Foxes are looking for a return to the Championship at the first time of asking after being relegated last season.

McLean: "I think that it's been difficult for Russell to come into a club that over the past couple of seasons has been on a constant decline and there's been a huge turnover of players.

"His biggest challenge is changing the environment and the mindset of the players. He's also at a club where there's huge pressure being in League One. For a club of that magnitude it's unacceptable.

"So I think it's going to probably take a little bit longer than I'm sure he would like. But at the same time I'm under no illusions, I feel that he is the right man for the job and you just hope that he's given the time to be able to turn things around."

'That's a sackable performance' - what next for Martin at Leicester?

Oxford Utd thump Leicester to heap pressure on Martin

Following a much-needed 4-0 win over high-flying Charlton at the bet365, which lifted them into mid-table, Stoke City are looking to push on after a poor start to the season.

McLean: "A brilliant result for Stoke up against Charlton who potentially could've gone top of the league today after having a great start themselves.

"I think that was a real statement of intent, the manner in which they beat them and that's back-to-back wins for them now, first against a Norwich side that I feel haven't got going yet but will do and a Charlton side who've had a good start to the season.

"I think the recruitment has been good in the summer. Ethan Galbraith was a brilliant signing for them, and hopefully they can continue to build and start to fulfil some of the promise that we've expected from them for the past few seasons."

Stoke hit four to end Charlton's unbeaten start

Alex Neil's Millwall are one of the most unpredictable clubs in the top four divisions. After five games the Lions have lost two matches and won three, including Saturday's emphatic 4-0 victory over Bolton at The Den, which also saw two late red cards.

McLean: "Millwall never seem to draw. They had a brilliant start to the season, wining their first two games then back-to-back defeats, but they're very much back on the horse today after a magnificent performance.

"I fully expect them to be in the shake up at the end of the season. I think that they are a team where it's all or nothing. They will win plenty of games and they will lose a few along the way, but I think that they've got more than enough in the squad to be competing."

Late Dykes double seals Millwall win over Bolton

Burnley sit bottom of the Championship, having been playing against the giants of English football in the Premier League less than six months ago. Their hopes of a first win of the season were squashed late on with Bristol City scoring two goals in the final 10 minutes at Turf Moor.

McLean: "They need to find some kind of cohesion and togetherness at the moment. They just look like a team that's been relegated and a team that is still suffering from the hangover of last season.

"Obviously with a new manager [Nicky Hayen], he needs to get his message across to the boys as he needs to get some kind of confidence into them, but the only way they're going to do that is by sticking together and grinding out a result.

"I think once they get their first win on the board and start to get a little bit of confidence they have got good players in their squad. I think Hayen needs to be given a bit of time. It's far too early in this season to be making decisions on a manager's future."

Bristol City hit late winner to leave Burnley bottom

Ian Holloway has got Swindon Town flying in League Two. They currently sit second behind Bristol Rovers with three wins in their past four matches, with Aaron Drinan's hat-trick securing a 3-1 home victory over Colchester on Saturday.

McLean: "I'm confident that Swindon will do really well this season. I think they'll be really disappointed that they didn't make the play-offs last year. They just missed out and hit a really bad patch of form at the wrong time.

"But I think with a striker like Aaron Drinan, who got a hat-trick today and scored 22 league goals last season, I expect him to probably get even more than that this season. And with the experience they had from last year, I expect them to be fully challenging for automatic promotion this season."

Aaron McLean was speaking to BBC Sport England's Ben Marvell.

title: Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble
description: Taylor Fritz and Flavio Cobolli lose in the third round as six top-10 seeds are knocked out of the men's singles in the first week at the US Open.
fullText:
Taylor Fritz was unable to explain how he let a two-set lead slip against Francisco Cerundolo as he became one of six top-10 seeds to be eliminated from the men's draw in the first week of the US Open.

The American ninth seed was in complete control and went an early break up in the third set, only for Argentina's Cerundolo to produce a shock 3-6 4-6 6-3 6-4 6-4 win to reach the fourth round.

Less than an hour later, fifth seed Flavio Cobolli of Italy fell to a 7-6 (7-4) 3-6 0-6 3-6 defeat by Belgium's Alexander Blockx, opening up the men's draw even further.

"I don't even know what to say," Fritz said. "I don't really want to talk to anybody, see anybody.

"I need to get out for a couple days and then get back to work. I don't know how I let that happen today."

Cerundolo and 28th seed Blockx will now meet in the fourth round with a place in the quarter-finals up for grabs.

This year's biggest shock at Flushing Meadows was also the first, as Novak Djokovic was beaten by Argentina's Mariano Navone on the opening day's play.

Fourth seed Djokovic was eyeing an historic 25th Grand Slam title but was left in tears after a five-set loss to the world number 49.

Next to go was 10th seed Arthur Fils. The Frenchman was another first-round casualty as he went down in four sets against former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas of Greece.

The highest seed ousted thus far is Canada's Felix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed, who lost to Karen Khachanov in round two, the same stage at which sixth seed Alex de Minaur was beaten.

Those exits looked to have cleared the way for Fritz and Cobolli to go deep into the tournament, but it was an opportunity neither were able to take.

For Fritz, a finalist at Flushing Meadows in 2024, the frustration is all the greater at his home Slam.

He was bidding to become the fifth American through to the fourth round at this year's tournament. With no Jannik Sinner to contend with and Carlos Alcaraz only recently returned from a wrist injury, excitement was growing that, 23 years on from Andy Roddick's US Open triumph, there may finally be another home winner in the men's singles.

That chance persists - but Fritz will know he has let a golden opportunity slip.

Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory

Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open

The chance of a maiden Grand Slam title has also escaped Cobolli for another few months after his capitulation against Blockx.

Having edged the first set on a tie-break, the Italian lost his way and after surrendering the third set to love in just 20 minutes, could not recover.

"I think my energy was a little bit lower than the other days," he said. "I feel a little bit more tight and maybe more tired."

Cobolli admitted Blockx deserved the win and would support him in the next round.

"Alex is very good guy outside the court. He deserved to win, and he won," he added.

Defeats for Cobolli and Fritz mean that apart from top seed Alexander Zverev, only two top-20 players remain in the top half of the draw in 14th seed Learner Tien and 17th seed Jakub Mensik - and they play one another on Friday.

It means Zverev could feasibly reach the final without playing a top-10 player and will not have to face anyone in the top 20 before the semis.

In the men's doubles, British pair Arthur Fery and Joshua Paris progressed with a 6-4 5-7 6-4 win over Anirudh Chandrasekar of India and Ivan Liutarevich of Belarus.

Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison, the fifth seeds, also advanced as they beat French duo Arthur Reymond and Luca Sanchez 6-0 7-6 (7-3).

But there was disappointment for David Stevenson and Marcus Willis as they lost 5-7 7-6 (7-2) 6-3 to France's 11th seeds Sadio Doumbia and Fabien Reboul.

title: Fans boo as MVP wins in underwhelming UFC farewell
description: Michael 'Venom' Page's last fight on his UFC contract ends in an underwhelming win against Nursulton Ruziboev amid booing fans in Paris.
fullText:
Michael 'Venom' Page's last fight on his UFC contract ended in an underwhelming win against Nursulton Ruziboev amid booing fans in Paris.

London's Page, who is nicknamed 'MVP', landed a handful of eye-catching strikes during the contest but could not deliver the knockout that the fans craved as he won by unanimous decision.

The 39-year-old's victory means all five of his wins in the UFC since joining in 2024 have come via decision.

Page joined the UFC with a reputation as an innovative striker with a resume of highlight-reel knockouts, but admitted pre-fight he has underperformed since joining the organisation.

Page said the fight with Uzbekistan's Ruziboev was "important to re-establish myself with the UFC", but he did not get the finish he wanted.

Page, who arrived in the UFC over two years ago with 13 knockouts to his name, received a raucous ovation from the French crowd as he entered the octagon.

Ruziboev controlled the majority of the first round on the ground before Page started to open up midway through the fight.

He landed a kick to Ruziboev's knee which wobbled the 32-year-old, before smiling and showboating as he delivered a number of feints.

Page delivered an overhead right and an elbow, but the explosive moments were few and far between as the crowd grew frustrated at a lack of action.

Throughout the bout, Page landed only 12 significant strikes to Ruziboev's eight.

Page has shown throughout his UFC career he is a master of movement and evasion, without having the finishing instinct that the most successful fighters possess.

The fight against Ruziboev followed the same pattern, and although Page was awarded victory by the judges, his arm was raised after jeers from the crowd.

With Page now a free agent, potential options for him if he does not re-sign with the UFC include joining the PFL or turning to boxing.

In the main event, French-Moroccan Salahdine Parnasse earned a stunning first-round TKO win over Dan Hooker.

Parnasse was making his UFC debut and delivered in front of a home crowd, landing a punishing kick to the body before dropping New Zealand's Hooker with a left hook.

The 28-year-old followed with a flurry of punches as Hooker, ranked 12 in the lightweight division, shelled up on the floor, forcing the referee to wave off the contest.

There was also victory for fellow Briton Kurtis Campbell, who submitted American Trevor Peek in the third round of their featherweight bout via a rear-naked choke.

It was a return to winning ways for the 24-year-old Liverpudlian, who lost on his UFC debut to Danny Silva in March.

Campbell's win extends his professional record to nine wins and one defeat.

"I know my debut didn't go the way I wanted it to but I'm here to show I'm the real deal and the future is bright," said Campbell.

Earlier on the card, London's Nathaniel Wood lost by unanimous decision to Moldova's Pavel Andrusca, bringing his four-fight win streak to an end.

Andrusca, who was a late replacement after Wood's original opponent Mairon Santos withdrew 10 days prior to the fight, extended the unbeaten start to his career to nine.

At UFC 322 on 3 October in Salt Lake City, it was announced Brazil's Natalia Silva will fight for the vacant flyweight title against China's Wang Cong.

Former title holder Valentina Shevchenko has vacated the belt and is set to miss over a year with injury, according to the UFC.

title: Wrexham boss Parkinson says Swansea captain should have seen red
description: The Wrexham boss claimed the Wales international's challenge on Callum O'Hare was a 'leg-breaker'
fullText:
Wrexham manager Phil Parkinson says Swansea City captain Ben Cabango got away with a "leg-breaking challenge" in their Welsh derby stalemate.

Parkinson claimed the Wales defender should have been given a straight red for the lunge on midfielder Callum O'Hare late on in the match at the Swansea.com Stadium.

Cabango, who had come on as a second-half substitute, was booked for the foul that prompted an angry reaction from the visitors' bench.

O'Hare was replaced soon after as Swansea maintained their unbeaten start to the season to stay top of the early Championship table.

"I know we want to protect our players but, when someone flies in at that speed, that could have been a leg-breaking challenge," Parkinson said.

"I thought the referee handled the atmosphere well, but in the big decision he didn't make the right call.

"I don't think anybody in the ground or whether people watching back on TV can deny that."

Swansea stay unbeaten but are frustrated by Wrexham in Welsh derby

Eyes on big prize as Swansea and Wrexham collide

More to come from Swansea, insists Matos

Cabango missed the ball in the 77th minute challenge and caught O'Hare, who was making his debut after a £6.5m deadline day move from Sheffield United.

Swansea boss Vitor Matos did not want to get involved in the debate after the game, saying: "I never comment on ref decisions, in one way or the other. If he [Parkinson] says that, good for him."

O'Hare claimed Cabango should have been sent off, saying the 16-cap centre-back told him he "didn't touch" the midfielder.

Parkinson added: "Cabango grabbed Kieffer around the neck on the halfway line before that. A yellow card and then the tackle.

"The same referee has sent Callum Doyle off against Oxford last season for a tackle, which maybe he was slightly out of control.

"But I'm very interested to ask the referee when he compares both those incidents. How he differentiates between the two, because every year, managers have to sit and listen to the referees about what they deem to be red cards, and when you're out of control, like Ben Cabango was and endangering a player. That is a straight red card."

Wrexham still had chances to win the game, but Parkinson said he was pleased with the efforts of his side on the back of a first win of the season, Wednesday's midweek triumph at Millwall.

"I thought we'd got better as the game went on and you know, we looked at an experienced team with a lot of football intelligence to like," said Parkinson, whose side welcome Burnley on Tuesday before a trip to West Ham United on Friday.

"You've got to stay in games with the offensive kind of bravery in situations, but also concentration levels and I thought in the last two games we've done that really well and we can take a lot of credit for that."

title: Humphries beats Greaves as Littler also wins
description: Luke Humphries and Luke Littler came through their second round matches to progress at the Czech Open on the European Tour.
fullText:
Luke Humphries and Luke Littler came through their second round matches to progress at the Czech Open on the European Tour.

Humphries ended the challenge of Beau Greaves, who had become the first woman to win a match on the European Tour with her first round win over Daryl Gurney.

The world number two averaged nearly 109 as he beat the three-time women's World Matchplay champion 6-2 in Prague.

"She's an amazing player, she pushed me all the way, it was a couple of bits towards the end of the match that got me through in the end," said Humphries, who will play Andrew Gilding in the third round.

"She's just a great dart player. If I had lost today, I wouldn't have been disgraced, I would have lost to a really great dart player."

World number one Littler had missed the last eight events on the European Tour and marked his return with a 6-4 victory against Germany's Niko Springer.

Littler, who won the men's World Matchplay title in July but was beaten by Brendan Dolan in the semi-finals of a Players Championship event last month, had a 108.59 average in his win.

"It's been a while since I've been to a European Tour," said Littler, who will next play Krzysztof Ratajski.

"Full credit to Niko. I was 5-2 up and then suddenly it was 5-4 and he was right back in it.

"I've just produced a 108 average, but when I was practising backstage I couldn't hit anything."

Michael van Gerwen and Gian van Veen also reached the last 16 with respective wins against Mario Vandenbogaerde and Jeffrey de Graaf.

title: Jones stuns Trump to set up final against Selby
description: Jak Jones earns a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open, and will face Mark Selby in the final.
fullText:
Jak Jones earned a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open and will face Mark Selby in the final.

Jones produced breaks of 95 and 68 on the way to a 3-1 lead before Trump levelled the match at 3-3.

However, Jones knocked in a 59 and a 52 to go 5-3 in front and, after England's Trump missed a green on the colours in a lengthy ninth frame, the Welshman secured victory.

"I started off quite well before the interval and then after that I started missing a few, didn't I?" Jones, beaten finalist in the 2024 World Championship, told Channel 5.

"I can't say I'm in this position a lot so it's a bit different for me compared to Judd."

Meanwhile, Selby came through a hard-fought win against fellow Englishman Liam Highfield, who was playing in his first ranking event semi-final.

Highfield took the opening frame before Selby levelled with an 85 and moved into a 3-2 lead.

A 56 helped Highfield level at 3-3, but Selby took three frames in a row to secure a 6-3 victory and a place in his 40th ranking event final.

"It was a tough match, Liam didn't make it easy for me at all," said Selby, who can climb from fourth to second in the rankings if he wins the title.

"His safety was incredible. I can't remember him playing a poor safety shot all the way through the match."

He added: "To think, when I was starting out, a 16-year-old kid in 1999, if somebody had said I'd get to 40 ranking finals, I'd have said 'no chance'. I'd have been happy to get to just one or two."

title: Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open
description: Coco Gauff reaches the US Open fourth round but last year's finalist Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys go out on a mixed day for home hopes.
fullText:
Coco Gauff marched into the fourth round of the US Open but compatriots Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys exited on a mixed day for home hopes in New York.

Gauff, the most recent American champion in New York in 2023, did not have things all her own way but maintained her bid for a second triumph by overcoming Spain's Cristina Bucsa 6-3 6-4.

However, Keys said she felt "scared" as she slumped to defeat despite leading her third set against China's Zheng Qinwen 5-0, while last year's runner-up Anisimova lost in straight sets.

There could yet be as many as five American women in the last 16, with Iva Jovic hoping to join Gauff, Jessica Pegula, Taylor Townsend and Emma Navarro in the fourth round.

American players could also contest six of the eight fourth-round matches in the men's draw, with Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe, Tommy Paul and Alex Michelsen through - and Learner Tien and Michael Zheng still to play.

Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory

Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble

Despite the weight of expectation that she has had to deal with from a young age at her home major, the 22-year-old Gauff is through to the second week at the US Open for a fifth successive year.

Gauff, who became the first American teenager to win the US Open since Serena Williams in 1999 with her breakthrough major success three years ago, heads into the fourth round as the form player in the women's game.

Victory over Bucsa was the 2025 French Open winner's eighth straight-set WTA Tour-level win in a row.

The fourth round is where Gauff's US Open challenge ended in the previous two editions, and she admitted that she struggled to handle the pressure last year.

But in recovering from a 3-1 deficit in the first set, and producing an immediate response to being broken to love in the second, Gauff demonstrated she is better placed to cope with that this time.

"I feel like I'm used to getting to the second week now. I woke up today and I was like 'oh we're already in round three'," Gauff said.

"There's expectations, being American, and I want to do well in front of the fans.

"Last year, I put so much pressure on myself. I'm enjoying the experience out here."

Keys appeared on course for a first fourth-round appearance at her home slam since 2023 after taking a commanding third set lead against Olympic champion Zheng.

But the 2025 Australian Open winner would miss a match point and lose each of the final seven games in a 1-6 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 loss that stunned the crowd.

The 31-year-old Keys said she felt as though she "couldn't play tennis anymore" in the final set.

"I obviously got off to a really good lead, and then I got really scared, like I couldn't swing [the racquet]," Keys said.

"I felt like I couldn't play tennis anymore. It just felt like it was a much bigger deal than just playing a tennis match all of a sudden."

Keys, who lost the 2017 US Open final to fellow American Sloane Stephens, went out in the fourth round at the other three majors in 2026.

"I feel like I've been struggling for a while now. I'm going to have to make some sort of changes," Keys said.

"I just kind of keep putting it off because that's how the tennis world works. It's just to the point where I actually need to do something about it."

Anisimova, beaten by world number one Aryna Sabalenka in last year's US Open final, lost in straight sets to Russian-born Austrian 24th seed Anastasia Potapova.

The 25-year-old was visibly frustrated with herself throughout the contest, losing her serve twice in the first set and four times in a topsy-turvy second.
